tasks.title: HTML parse on a cooperative task stack exhausts the stack and kills the process
tasks.evidence_before: Without any sanitizer: `swift test --filter AUDITDiagnosticsTests/testD_deepNestingThresholdWithoutASan` survives depth 1000 (clean malformedResponse) and DIES at depth 5000 with signal 10 (SIGBUS); `testE_deepNestingThroughHTMLExtraction` dies at depth 20000. With ASan the same failure appears at much lower depths and as a BUS in _platform_memset on a cooperative task (Task 3), which is how it was first found: `swift test --sanitize=address --filter ProviderContractTests/testDuckDuckGoTaxonomy` => signal 6. Attribution matrix: ScraperSupport.parse synchronously on the junk body = ok; DDG provider async on the same body = crash; DDG provider async on well-formed empty HTML = ok; TSan clean.
tasks.fix_summary: (1) MarkupDepth.containsMarkup rejects a body with no markup at all before parsing (ScraperSupport throws malformedResponse(provider)); scoped to the scrapers, because the web_open extractor must keep accepting plain text, JSON and YAML. (2) MarkupDepth.exceedsLimit counts element nesting iteratively on the raw bytes with an early exit and a cap of 512 (maximumNesting): comments, declarations, void elements, self-closing tags and raw-text element content (script/style/...) open no level, a '>' in a quoted attribute does not end a tag, a stray '<' is text. Exceeding it throws the new SearchError.markupDepthExceeded(limit), category .malformedResponse. (3) LargeStackParse.run executes the recursive part of ScraperSupport.parse and HTMLExtractor.extract on a dedicated 8 MiB-stack thread, synchronously, publishing the outcome through a Sendable OSAllocatedUnfairLock (no @unchecked Sendable, no unsynchronised shared state, deadlock-free because the parse thread does no Swift concurrency work). (4) Tests/WebSearchCoreTests/MarkupDepthTests.swift: 19 tests, including the three original probe inputs as assertions and a 512-deep document parsed via Task.detached; the temporary AUDITDiagnosticsTests.swift probes were deleted in the same commit. No byte cap added: the measured inputs are 25 KB and 100 KB, so size does not bound depth.
tasks.evidence_after: swift test --sanitize=address --filter 'MarkupDepthTests|ProviderContractTests|HTMLExtractorTests' => 81 tests, 0 failures, exit 0 (the run that previously ended in AddressSanitizer: BUS), including a 512-deep document parsed on a cooperative task. swift test --filter 'MarkupDepthTests|HTMLExtractorTests|FetchFallbackTests|FetchBehaviorTests' => 45 tests, 0 failures. Full suite swift test => 390 tests, 6 skipped, 0 failures (baseline 371/6, so +19 regression tests). swift build and swift build -c release => 0 warnings, 0 errors (baseline 0). Artifact: AUDIT/evidence/A01-asan.txt. Removing either the depth guard or the large-stack hop makes MarkupDepthTests kill the runner again (SIGBUS / signal 4).
tasks.notes: Reachability: web_open parses arbitrary attacker-controlled pages; the scraper path is opt-in but enabled in some deployments. Depth 5000 is ~25 KB of markup, 20000 is ~100 KB, both far below the 4 MiB response cap, so size limits do not bound depth; body size is capped where bodies are read. Item (3) of the fix was promoted from belt-and-braces to load-bearing by measurement: with the depth cap alone, a document AT the cap still overflowed a cooperative task stack under AddressSanitizer. Rather than lower the cap until the instrument was satisfied (which would make a production parameter depend on a debug build), the parse got a stack with room for the bound.

tasks.title: The HTTP transport serves exactly one MCP session per process, and that session can never be released
tasks.evidence_before: `main.swift` builds a single `StatefulHTTPServerTransport` at startup and hands it to `HTTPMCPHost`; that SDK type is one-shot. In the pinned MCP SDK 0.12.1, `StatefulHTTPServerTransport.handleInitializationRequest` rejects re-initialization — `if sessionID != nil { … .invalidRequest("Bad Request: Session already initialized") }` — and `handleRequest` returns `404 "Not Found: Session has been terminated"` for every request once `terminate()` has set `terminated = true`, while `terminate()` never clears `sessionID`. So a second or reconnecting HTTP client can never initialize, for the whole lifetime of the process. `HTTPMCPHost.dispatch` makes it worse by refusing GET and DELETE before the transport (`guard method == .POST else { … ("Allow", "POST") }`), so the SDK's DELETE termination path is unreachable and the dead session cannot even be released; the comment there ("Only POST is meaningful to the stateless transport") is also factually wrong, because the wired transport is `StatefulHTTPServerTransport`. `Tests/WebSearchCoreTests/HTTPTransportTests.swift:459-474` currently asserts the 405/`Allow: POST` behaviour, so a fix must update that test too.
tasks.fix_summary: HTTPMCPHost now keeps a session registry: a SessionFactory supplied by main.swift builds a fresh Server + StatefulHTTPServerTransport per initialize, and POST/GET/DELETE are routed by the Mcp-Session-Id the SDK issues (looked up with the SDK's case-insensitive request.header(_:)). A DELETE answered with 200 releases the session — transport disconnected, server stopped — so the process can serve the next client, and a refused initialize releases the half-built session. A request with no usable session is now 400 (no session id, not an initialize) or 404 (unknown/released id) instead of 405 Allow: POST. main.swift parks in host.waitUntilStopped() and stop() releases every live session before the event loop group shuts down.
tasks.evidence_after: Fails-before: with the pre-fix sources restored from HEAD and the new tests in place, testTwoClientsEachGetTheirOwnSession fails (second initialize -> 400, identical session id) and testDeletingASessionReleasesItAndAllowsReconnecting fails (DELETE -> 405, released-id request -> 200, reconnect -> 400 with the same id). After the fix: HTTPTransportTests 9 tests 0 failures (3 new); full suite 413 tests / 6 skipped / 0 failures; debug and release builds with -warnings-as-errors 0 warnings; swift-format --strict 0; swiftlint --strict exit 0; coverage 85.1 % >= 80 (unchanged, because the session code runs in the server subprocess — the gap A04 records). tasks.title: `Terminal.truncate` counts ANSI escape characters as display width, so truncating styled text can drop the SGR reset

  a CSI sequence except `ESC` a width of 1 — while its sibling `displayWidth`
  (`Terminal.swift:116-136`) skips escape sequences entirely and is documented as the width
  contract ("*Counts ANSI escape sequences as zero width, which matters because styled text is
  padded after colouring*"). The two disagree, so `Renderer` can (and at narrow widths does)
  cut a styled line inside a colour run and return it without the `\u{1B}[0m` that closes it;
  the colour then bleeds into the following columns and lines. Worked example with the exact
  algorithm: `truncate("\u{1B}[91m" + 40 × "x" + "\u{1B}[0m", to: 10)` consumes
  `ESC [ 9 1 m` (4 counted units) plus 5 `x`, then stops at the limit — the result is
  `"\u{1B}[91mxxxxx…"` with **no reset**, so everything after it is red. Cuts *inside* a
  sequence are equally reachable at other widths (stopping after `\u{1B}[9` leaves an
  unterminated CSI). No test covers styled truncation: `TerminalLayoutTests` truncates plain
  text only, and `testNoLineExceedsTerminalWidth` asserts only `displayWidth`, which passes
  with a dropped reset.
tasks.notes:
raw record: AUDIT/findings/L1-L2.md L2-9 · expected-correct: `truncate` must measure with the same escape-aware width as `displayWidth`

  must guarantee balanced SGR in its output — e.g. re-append `\u{1B}[0m` when the input carried

So `mcps-mon --node n1=… --no-nodes` still probes n1, while `--no-nodes` alone disables probing; the two flags are order-independent in the usage text but order-dependent in the code. This is the same class of defect as the already-fixed order-dependent server transport flags, in a second parser.
tasks.notes: raw record: AUDIT/findings/L3-placeholders.md L3-29 · expected-correct: Track a `nodesDisabled` flag and make it authoritative after the loop, or document that `--node` wins. · confidence: certain

tasks.title: `--node` accepts a relative URL and can swallow the next flag as its value
tasks.evidence_before: `guard let url = URL(string: urlText)` is not an absolute-URL check — `URL(string:)` accepts relative references — so `--node n1=foo` starts, probes nothing useful and shows `n1 DOWN … unreachable` instead of a CLI error. `value(for:)` returns `arguments[index + 1]` without checking that it is not itself a flag, so `--node --interval=5` creates a node literally named `--interval` and consumes the interval flag. The identical `value(for:)` is copy-pasted into `TransportConfiguration.parse`, where `--host --http-path` likewise accepts `--http-path` as a host string and fails only at bind time.

tasks.title: A request-head `Content-Length` reserves up to 1 MiB per connection before any body arrives
tasks.evidence_before: `bodyBuffer.reserveCapacity(min(head.headers.first(name: "content-length").flatMap(Int.init) ?? 4096, 1 << 20))` runs on `.head`, i.e. on an untrusted header, and NIO's `ByteBuffer.reserveCapacity` allocates immediately when the requested capacity exceeds the current one. A client can make the server hold ~1 MiB per connection by sending only the request head with `Content-Length: 1048576` and no body; the 1 MiB cap in `HTTPMCPHandler.maximumBodyBytes` is enforced only later, once bytes actually arrive. Bounded on the loopback default, but real for the opt-in unauthenticated non-loopback bind.
tasks.notes: raw record: AUDIT/findings/L3-placeholders.md L3-36 · expected-correct: Reserve a small fixed capacity (or grow lazily as `.body` parts arrive) and rely on the existing `maximumBodyBytes` check as the enforcement point. · confidence: likely

tasks.title: `mcp_smoke.py` de-chunks an SSE body after decoding it to `str`
tasks.evidence_before: `http_exchange` decodes the whole response first (`text = raw.decode("utf-8", "replace")`, `:296`) and then, for a chunked body, slices `remaining[index + 2 : index + 2 + size]` where `size` is the hex byte count from the chunk header (`:315`). A byte count is applied to a `str`, so any non-ASCII body (Swift's `JSONEncoder` emits raw UTF-8) shifts every later boundary and the recovered stream is truncated/corrupted. Latent today only because the smoke payloads are ASCII.
tasks.notes: raw record: AUDIT/findings/L3-placeholders.md L3-39 · expected-correct: De-chunk the raw bytes before decoding, or let `http.client`/`urllib` handle framing. · confidence: certain (mismatch), uncertain (reachability today)

tasks.title: HTTP smoke can wait 20 s on a dead server and never checks that it is alive

tasks.evidence_before:
```bash

NONINTERACTIVE=1 /bin/bash -c \
    "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)" \
    >/tmp/brew-install.log 2>&1 \

```
```bash

    say "loading searxng image from /tmp/searxng-image.tar"
    docker load -i /tmp/searxng-image.tar >/tmp/docker-load.log 2>&1 \
```

Every log target is a fixed name under the shared, world-writable `/tmp` (`:71, :96, :105, :151, :243, :247, :261, :280`) opened with plain `>` truncation, so a local attacker who pre-creates a path as a symlink can have the provisioning run (an account with cached sudo) truncate or clobber a file it can write. More interesting is `/tmp/searxng-image.tar`: `docker load` trusts the tarball's content, and the guard in front of it (`docker image inspect "${SEARXNG_IMAGE}"`, `:239`) only proves the *reference* is absent — a load that succeeds for a different image then makes `docker run "${SEARXNG_IMAGE}"` fail, but a tarball carrying the same reference is not obviously re-verified against the pinned digest, and the resulting container is run with the node's settings mounted read-only and publishes a port. Preconditions: local access to the node's `/tmp` dur …

Do not drop the digest pin or the canary to make this easier. · confidence: likely

tasks.title: A cross-scheme redirect is refused by the transport, not by our policy, and surfaces as an opaque transport error
tasks.discovered_by: Phase D, found while fixing B02 (probe with a readable /etc/hosts)
tasks.evidence_before: Probe: a loopback server answers 302 with Location: file:///etc/hosts. FileManager.isReadableFile(/etc/hosts) == true. The fetcher throws fetchFailed(entryURL, reason: 'the transport reported error -1102') — no file content is returned, and no .blockedURL is produced. URLSession/CFNetwork does not consult NoRedirectDelegate (willPerformHTTPRedirection) for a cross-scheme redirect, so it is refused (or attempted) below the manual loop and the manual loop's per-hop URLPolicy check never sees the hop. Same outcome for a readable temp file.
tasks.notes: Impact: the observable security outcome is correct (verified: no local content is returned even for a readable file), but the caller gets an opaque transport error instead of a policy denial, and the safety property rests on undocumented CFNetwork behaviour rather than on our policy. Candidate fix: curate the file-system transport codes in DirectHTTPFetcher's error mapping (-1100/-1101/-1102 => 'the server redirected to a local file, which is not fetched'), and state in URLPolicy's documentation that cross-scheme redirects are refused beneath us; keep the regression test that pins the observable outcome. raw record: found during B02 (not in a Phase B pass)
